title: Small Steps are not Atomisation
author: Kris Boulton
summary: Kris Boulton pushes back on a recurring criticism of his 'atomisation' approach to maths instruction — the objection that breaking mathematics into small procedural steps is pedagogically hollow — by arguing the criticism attacks something that isn't actually atomisation. He cites Colin Foster's critique as a genuine, non-strawman description of what many teachers believe atomisation means, but insists it describes only 'small steps': breaking a process into smaller pieces without revealing any underlying mathematical structure. Real atomisation, Boulton argues, means decomposing a cognitive routine into its constituent conceptual atoms — each atom a fact, concept, or further routine — communicated through an instruction, testing, and expansion sequence built on his five principles of instruction. He offers several worked examples (the distance from a parabola's axis of symmetry to its roots, why the sine rule works via the circumcircle, how the trapezium area formula degenerates into the triangle area formula) to show that atomisation, done properly, surfaces rich mathematical relationships that mere step-breakdown never touches. The piece functions as the opening entry in a planned Substack series unpacking atomisation's benefits and mechanics in more depth.
points: Boulton's central distinction: 'small steps' breaks a process into smaller pieces without revealing mathematical structure; 'atomisation' decomposes a cognitive routine into conceptual atoms (facts, concepts, or sub-routines) that do reveal structure.

He treats a published critique of 'atomisation' by Colin Foster as accurate about what teachers commonly practice under that name, but argues it isn't actually a critique of atomisation itself — a genuine 'lethal mutation' of the term.

Real atomisation requires that new atoms be taught through explicit instruction, testing, and expansion sequences built on 'the five principles of instruction,' not just chunked into smaller procedural pieces.

His worked examples (parabola axis-to-root distance, why the sine rule works via the circumcircle, trapezium-to-triangle area formula degeneration) are offered as concrete proof that atomisation surfaces mathematical relationships invisible to simple step-breakdown.
The post is explicitly positioned as the first in a multi-part series that will go on to catalogue 'a dozen benefits' of atomisation and how it delivers on them.
quotes: I felt a little annoyed at the time, so held back on publishing it. I felt annoyed not because atomisation was being criticised, but because it wasn't atomisation that was being criticised.
I think I haven't because atomisation isn't really about breaking processes down into small steps. So that objection wouldn't make sense; it would never come up.

The problem is that what Colin describes as 'atomisation' is not atomisation. I don't believe it's a straw man. I expect that what Colin describes here is what teachers really are doing when they say they are 'doing atomisation.' But it's not atomisation.
Did you know the reason the sine rule works is because each ratio describes the diameter of the triangles circumcircle? It's Atom 28 in our conceptual atomisation of the sine and cosine rules.

Did you know that if you shrink one parallel side of a trapezium, eventually you get a triangle? And, that if you enter a = 0 into the area formula for a trapezium, you get the area formula for a triangle?
Small steps doesn't reveal these relationships. Conceptual atomisation does. Routine atomisation provides the opportunity to explore then in depth.
